newsitem.title: USA: White House says database not used for fundraising.
newsitem.headline: White House says database not used for fundraising.

text.p: The White House on Thursday denied that its computerized database had been used to raise money for President Bill Clinton's re-election campaign or for any other unauthorised purposes.

Responding to published reports that Clinton political operatives used the computerized White House list to track Democratic Party contributors, White House spokesman Barry Toiv told reporters: "We have no knowledge that it was ever used for any unofficial purpose."
"There was clear guidance as to how the database could be used, and the guidance was it could only be used for official purposes," Toiv said.

The Los Angeles Times reported on Thursday that the database was set up with federal funds in 1994 at the direction of the president and his wife, Hillary, and that White House staff frequently retrieved data on large political contributors and turned it over to the Democratic National Committee to help raise money for Clinton's re-election.
But Mrs. Clinton, in an interview with a small group of reporters, said she knew very little about it.

"As I understand it, the computer database was put into place to keep track of events and people associated with the official business of the White House. Insofar as I know, that was how it was used," she said.
"I would doubt that I was the person who ordered it," Mrs. Clinton added. "It struck me as something we needed ... and that's all I know about it."
DNC Press Secretary Amy Weiss Tobe issued a statement saying that "to our knowledge, there was no use of the White House database by DNC officials or employees."
Both The Los Angeles Times and Time magazine said that a former DNC finance chairman, Texas oilman Truman Arnold, used the database.

Time said it "helped him (Arnold) ensure that major donors were accorded a fair share of presidential perks, a reward system of (White House) Lincoln bedroom sleepovers, foreign trips and government postings that helped the party hit a DNC fundraising record of $125 million last year."
Arnold declined requests for interviews but issued a statement saying he was "very proud of the accomplishments" during his tenure.

"As to the information technology at this time -- I do not know. Not being computer literate, the gathering of information came from multiple sources by our staff," he said, adding that he "never heard" of the White House database until references to it appeared in Time magazine.
Toiv said the White House counsel's office had spoken to Arnold and that even after that, the White House was still confident it could assert that the database was not misused.
A congressional subcommittee led by Representative David McIntosh, an Indiana Republican, was looking into the matter.

McIntosh's investigation was one of several probes into questionable Clinton campaign fund-raising tactics, which first stirred a commotion late last year when it was revealed that the Democrats had solicited large sums from Asian business interests with a stake in U.S. trade policy.

At a news conference on Tuesday, Clinton conceded "mistakes were made" in raising money for his bid for a second four-year term, but he insisted contributors did not buy influence with him and said the system was not corrupt.

"I don't think there is anything wrong with raising money for the political process," Clinton said, adding that, "What happens is, there is a race to get as much money as you can to keep from being buried by the other people ... and at the edges, errors are made."

Clinton supports a pending campaign finance reform bill that would place new limits on political fundraising. Its chief sponsors are Sens. John McCain, an Arizona Republican, and Russell Feingold, a Wisconsin Democrat.
